div.stage: Enter Dionysus on foot dressed in the skin of the Nemean Lion, and the club of Heracles in his hand, and Xanthias heavily laden on a donkey.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Master, should I tell one of those usual jokes
which always make the audience laugh?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: By Zeus, say what you want—except “I'm hard pressed”
Forget that one, it's really quite annoying.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Nothing else witty either?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Anything but “What a strain!”

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What then? Can I say the really funny one?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Of course,
Go right ahead—but don't let me catch you saying this.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That you must shift your pack to ease yourself.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, can't I say I've got such a load on me,
unless someone takes it off, I'll bust a gut?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Please don't, unless you wish to make me sick.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: So why should I have to carry all this stuff,
without doing any of the jokes that Phrynichus
and Lycis and Ameipsias always make
the baggage-carriers say in all their comedies?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Just don't. Since when I'm in the theater
and hear any of these stupid jokes,
I go away just older by a year.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Alas, poor wretched me! My neck
is really strained, but can't crack the joke.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now is this not outrage and utter insolence,
That I myself, Dionysos, son of Winejug,
must walk, and let this fellow ride,
so he might feel no pain and bear no burden?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What? I bear no burden?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How can you bear anything? You're riding.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: But I've got all this!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How so?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Most heavily!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: The weight you carry- isn't it carried by the donkey?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Absolutely not; not what I'm holding and carrying.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How can you carry, for God's sake, when you
yourself are carried by another?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I don't know, but my shoulder's sure hard pressed.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, since you say the donkey doesn't help,
Suppose you take your turn, and carry him.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Unhappy wretch! Why didn't I join the navy?
Then I'd tell you to whistle a different tune!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You scoundrel, get on down! Here's the door
I'm walking to, the first place
I must stop.—Ho, porter! porter there, I say.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Who banged the door? Like a Centaur
Someone drove into it. Say, what's this?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: My boy!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, what?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Didn't you notice?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No, what?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How afraid he was...

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: That you might lose your mind.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Oh, by Demeter, I can't help but laugh!
I'll bite my lip—but still I've got to laugh!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Come here, my good man. I need to ask you a favor.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: I just can't stifle this laughter,
seeing a lion's skin thrown over that saffron gown—
What does it mean? How have club and buskin joined forces?
Where in the world were you going?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I was on board of Cleisthenes.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: And were you at the naval battle?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Yes, and we sank some twelve or thirteen hostile ships.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: You two?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Aye, by Apollo.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And then I woke up!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And while I was on board, reading
the Andromeda, suddenly a craving
smote my heart, you'll never guess how strong.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: A craving? How big?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Small, like Molon.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: For a woman?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh no.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: A boy?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Not at all!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: A man?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Argh!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: You did it with Cleisthenes?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't make fun, brother, I've really got it bad,

div.l: Such passionate desire torments me so.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: What is it, little brother?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I can't explain.
But still I'll try to tell you in a riddle.
Did you ever feel a sudden urge for soup?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Soup! Yowee! Ten thousand times so far.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Have I made it clear, or should I try again?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Not about the soup, I fully comprehend.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, just so great a wish gnaws at me now—
For my Euripides.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: And dead, at that!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And now no mortal shall persuade me not to
Go after him.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: What, down to hell?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's right, and lower still if possible.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: With what intent?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I want a clever poet, for the race
is now extinct—all who survive are bad.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: What! Isn't Iophon alive?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, he's the only good thing left, if he's good at all. I don't even know for sure if that's the case.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Why don't you bring back Sophocles, Euripides' superior, if you've really got to take one?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Not before I take Iophon aside all by himself,
and test what he does without Sophocles. Besides, Euripides is such a scoundrel,
he might well try to run away with me,
but Sophocles was easy going here, and easy going there as well.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: And where is Agathon?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh, he has left us;
a decent poet, lamented by his friends.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Where has he gone?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: To the banquet of the Blest.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: And where's Xenoclees?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh, God! May he drop dead!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: What of Pythangelus?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No word of me,
long suffering with this shoulder ache of mine!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Surely you must have some other youngsters,
At least ten thousand tragic playwrights,
All babbling miles further than Euripides.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: These are but stunted offshoots and mere blatherings,
showcases of swallows, banes of The Art,
which disappear at once, if they get a single chorus,
just one chance to piss on tragedy.
You'll not find one creative poet,
if you looked, to bawl a noble sentiment.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Creative, how?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Creative like one who utters
some great risky phrase like this:
“The airy hall of Zeus”, or “foot of time”,
or “heart that would not swear by all that's holy”
and “tongue that swears, without consent of mind.”

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: This pleases you?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I'm crazy about it!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: I think it's trash. I'm sure you think so too.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't try to run my mind, mind your own business.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Well, I repeat, it just seems completely rubbish.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Teach me how to eat!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No word of me!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But this is why I have come in this getup
to look like you; so you would inform me who they were who took you in, in case I needed them, the ones you found down there when you went after Cerberus:
Describe to me the harbours, bakers' shops,
brothels, rest stops, detours, springs, and roads,
the towns, their customs, and the inns
Where there are fewest bugs.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No word of me!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Why, you rash fellow, will you too dare to go?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: No more of that, but tell me
Which of the roads will bring us quickest down to Hell,
And one that's not too hot, nor yet too cold.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Well, let me see, which shall I tell you first, which one?
There's one starting with a cord and stool,
Just hang yourself!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Stop—that's suffocation.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Well here's another short well-beaten track,
The pestle and mortar route.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You mean hemlock!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Too cold and wintry.
Your shins freeze off immediately.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Well, shall I tell you of a quick and downhill path?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh yes, I'm really no great walker.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Just slip on down to Ceramicus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Then what?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Climb up onto the top of the tower.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And do what?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: From there observe the torch race starting up,
And when the spectators cry “The're off!”
You go off too.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Go where?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Below.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But then I'd lose the two dolmades of my brain!
I'd never go that way.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: How will you go?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: The road you went.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: It's a hell of a haul.
Right off you'll come to an enormous lake,
A fathomless abyss!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How will I get across?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: In a little boat—just so big!—an aged mariner will take you over, and take two obols for your fare.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Bah, how powerful those two obols everywhere!
How'd they get there?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Theseus introduced them.
And after this you'll see ten thousand snakes
And terrible wild beasts.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't frighten me or make me scared.
You won't turn me aside

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Then a great slough
of ever-flowing dung, and in it lie
any who ever wronged his guest,
or screwed a boy and took back the pay,
Or thrashed his mother, or smacked his father's jaw,
or swore a perjured oath,
Or copied out a speech of Morsimus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now, by the Gods, besides these there should be
Whoever learned Kinesias' pyrrhic dance.

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: Next a breath of pipes will surround you,
you'll see a shining light, just like up here,
then myrtle groves, and happy choirs
of men and woman mixed who loudly clap their hands.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And who are these?

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: These are the Mystic celebrants.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: By God, I am the donkey at the Mysteries!
But I won't put up with this for one more minute!

sp.speaker: Heracles
sp.l: And these will tell you all you wish to know,
For they live closest by the way to Pluto's door.
And now farewell, my brother.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Thanks, and you too
prosper. But you, take the baggage up again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What, before I've laid it down?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Yes, sir, at once.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No, please, I beg you, but hire someone
from the funeral party, who's coming just for this.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And if I don't find any?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Then I'll carry it.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's fair.
And sure enough, they're bringing out a corpse right here.
Hallo you there ! —you, the dead man, I mean;
Will you take this baggage down to Hell?

sp.speaker: Corpse
sp.l: How much is there?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: This here.

sp.speaker: Corpse
sp.l: Will you pay two drachmas?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: God no, less than that.

sp.speaker: Corpse
sp.l: Get out of the way, you!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Wait, my good man, maybe we can strike a bargain.

sp.speaker: Corpse
sp.l: If you don't put down two drachmas, no deal.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Come, take nine obols.

sp.speaker: Corpse
sp.l: I'd rather be alive again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: How arrogant this damned fellow is—drop dead!
I'll go myself.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You're tried and true.
Let's go to the boat.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Avast, lay her to.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What's this?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: This? The lake, of course,
the very one he mentioned, and now I see the boat.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Me too, by Poseidon, and this one here is Charon.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Ah Charon, Charon, cheery, cheery Charon!

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Who's bound for the retreat from strife and woe?
Who is for Lethe's plain? who comes for donkey's wool?
who for the Cerberians, or the crows, or Taenarus?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's me.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Then get in quick.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Where do you think we'll stop?
At the crows, really?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Absolutely, just for you.
Get in.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Here, boy.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: I will not take the Slave,
unless he fought at sea, to save his hide.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Oh God, not me—I happened to have an eye infection.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Then you must run around the lake.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: So where should I wait up?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: By the Stone of Withering
At the rest-stop.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You hear?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: O yes, I hear,
unhappy wretch, whom did I cross when I set out?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Sit down at the oar,
If anyone else is sailing, hurry up!
Hey, you, what are you doing?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What am I doing? What else but
sitting on the oar, where you commanded.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Come, fatso, just sit down there.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: See?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Grasp the oar, stretch out your hands.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: See?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Stop fooling around; lean your body forward,
And pull with a will.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How can I row?
Inexperienced, un-seafaring, unSalaminian.

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: It's easy. You'll hear songs
most delightful, when once you lay into it.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: From whom?

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: The marvelous music of the frogswans.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Then order away!

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Heave ho, heave ho—

sp.speaker: Chorus of Frogs
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax,
Brekekekex koax koax,
Marshy children of the waters,
the harmonious cry of hymns,
Let us sing, my sweet
song, Koaxkoax,
which for Nysian
Dionysos, son of Zeus,
we sang at Limnae
when in drunken revelry
at the Feast of the Jars
the crowd of people marches to my sanctuary.
Brekekekex koax koax,

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I'm starting to hurt
my butt, Koax koax!
Maybe it doesn't bother you!

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Go to hell with your koax
koax and nothing but koax!

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: Rightly so, you busybody.
the Muses of the fine lyre love us
And so does horn-crested Pan, playing his reed pipe.
And the harpist Apollo delights in us as well,
On account of the reed, which as a bridge for his lyre
I nourish in the water of the pond.
Brekekekex koax koax.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I've got blisters,
and for long now my rump's been sweating.
It's going to pop up and say—

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Song-loving brood,
Stop!

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: No, all the more
will we sing, if ever
On a sunshiny day,
we leaped through the weeds
and the rushes, rejoicing in the song's
diving melodies,
or fleeing Zeus' rain
at the bottom our watery dance—
song we sang
with bubbles and splashes.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax.
I'll just take this from you.

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: Ah, then we'll suffer horribly.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But I suffer worse,
if I explode as I row.

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Croak on—it doesn't bother me.

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: You bet we'll shout
as much as our throats
can hold, all day long.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Brekekekex koax koax.
You won't beat me with that.

sp.speaker: Frogs
sp.l: And you won't beat us at all.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Nor you me, oh no,
Never! For I will shout
if I have to, all day long,
until I vanquish you with this koax.
brekekekex koax koax.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I knew I'd finally stop you from ko-axing!

sp.speaker: Charon
sp.l: Stop, stop—now bring to with your oar,
Get out and pay your fare.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Here, two obols.
Oh, Xanthias—where is Xanthias? Hey, Xanthias!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Ahoy!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Come here.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Welcome, master.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What's this here?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Darkness and sludge.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Have you met here with any parricides
Or perjurers, as he told us?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Haven't you?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: By Poseidon, yes. l think I see some now.
Well now, what do we do next?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: We had best go on;
This is the place where wild beasts are,
That fellow said.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: He be hanged!
He was pretending, just to frighten me.
He knows that I'm a warrior, and he's jealous.
There's nothing quite so boastful as that Heracles.
Now I should only like to meet with some adventure,
To win some contest worthy of our trip.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Of course. Wait! I think I hear a noise.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Where, where is it?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Behind you.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Get behind me!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: But now it's in front.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Get in front then!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And now, by Zeus, l see a monstrous beast.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What kind?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: O horrible! it takes all kinds of shapes,
Now it's an ox, and now a mule, and now
A lovely woman.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Where is she? I'll go meet her.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Wait, now it's not a woman, but a bitch.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Why, this must be Empusa.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Ah! her whole face burns like fire.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Does she have a leg of bronze?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: By Poseidon, yes—and the other is cow dung,
Be sure of it.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Where can I escape?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And where can I?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh priest, preserve me now, to be your drinking buddy.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Oh! we are lost, my royal Heracles.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't call me that,
I beg you. Man, never use that name.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, Dionysus then.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's worse than the other.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, never mind, come on, my noble master.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Cheer up, we've done all right,
And we may say just like Hegelochus,
“And from the storm I see once more calm-ari.”
Empusa's gone.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You swear it?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: By Zeus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Swear it again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I swear by Zeus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: By Zeus!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Good grief, how I grew pale at the sight of her.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: But this thing of yours got stained reddish brown with fear.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Alas, why do these wretched ills befall me?
Now which of all the Gods shall I accuse of my destruction?
“The airy hall of Zeus, or foot of time?”
sp.stage: Sound of a pipe is heard within.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Hey!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What is it?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Didn't you hear?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Hear what?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: The puff of pipes.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Oh yes, and now a whiff
of torches wafted over me most mystically.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Let's crouch down here and listen silently.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: O Iacchus, Iacchus O,
O Iacchus, Iacchus O!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: This is it, Master. The band of initiates
are singing here, the ones he mentioned to us.
They're chanting Diagoras' Hymn to Iacchus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I think so too, so keeping quiet's
the best thing, so we can learn for sure.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Iacchus, here abiding in temples most reverend,
Iacchus, O Iacchus,
come to dance in this meadow;
to your holy mystic bands
Shake the leafy crown
around your head, brimming
with myrtle,
Boldly stomp your feet in time
to the wild fun-loving rite,
with full share of the Graces, the holy dance, sacred
to your mystics.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: O reverend mistress daughter of Demeter,
How sweet that roast pork smells to me!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Keep quiet, if you want to get a piece of sausage.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Awake, for it has come tossing torches in hand,
Iacchos, Oh Iacchos,
the light-bringing star of our nocturnal rite.
Now the meadow brightly burns
Old men's knees start to sway.
They shake away their pains
and the long cycles of ancient years
Through your holy rite.
Beaming with your torch,
lead forth to the flowering stretch of marsh
the youth that makes your choruses, o blessed one!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Let him be mute and stand aside from our sacred dances
who has no experience of mystical language, or has not cleansed his mind
Who never has seen and never has danced in the rites of the noble Muses
Nor ever has been inducted into the Bacchic mysteries of beef-eating Cratinus
Or who takes delight in foolish words when doing this is ill-timed,
Whoever does not eliminate hateful factionalism, and is disagreeable to the citizens,
but kindles and fans civil strife, in his thirst for private advantage:
Whoever takes bribes when guiding the state through the midst of a storm
Or betrays our forts or our ships, smuggles contraband from Aegina
As Thorycion did, that wretched collector of taxes
Sending pads and sails and pitch to Epidauros,
Or persuades anyone to send supplies to the enemies' ships,
Or defiles Hecate's shrine, while singing dithyrambs,
Or any politician who bites off the pay of the poets
For being ridiculed in the ancestral rites of Dionysus.
All these I warn, and twice I warn, and thrice I warn again,
stand aside from our mystical dances; but as for you: arouse the song
and the night-long dances, that belong to our festival here.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Each one boldly marches
to the flowery meadows and glens
stamping in time
jesting, joking
and mocking;
we've breakfasted enough.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: But onward now and nobly extol
The Saving goddess,
as you chant the melody,
she who claims to save our land as the seasons pass
even against Thorycion's will.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Come now, sing a different strain of hymn to the harvest queen,
the goddess Demeter, gracing her with sacred airs.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Demeter, mistress of our holy rites,
be present now
and preserve your song and dance.
And grant that I may sport and dance the livelong day in safety.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: and that I may say much that is funny and much that is serious
and, as befits your festival,
may I play and joke and win the day, and wear the victor's crown.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Now then
Summon the god of the hour with your songs
the partner of this dance of ours.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Iacchus, honored by all, deviser of our festal song
most sweet, follow us here
to the goddess and show us how
you travel a long road with ease.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, lead me onward,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: for as a joke and to save money you split my sandal
and rags, and found a way for us to sport and dance scot-free.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, lead me onward,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: For I just now caught a sidelong glance of a very cute girl,
a partner in our dance, and through a rip in her robe
I saw a titty peeping out.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, lead me onward.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, I'm always ready to join in the fun, and
I want to dance with her.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Me too!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Do you want to join together
and make fun of Archedemos?
When he was seven he hadn't grown citizen teeth

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: but now he's a big politician
amongst the corpses up above.
And he takes first prize for villainy.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And Cleisthenes I hear
among the tombstones
plucks his rear and rips his cheeks

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: beats his breast and bends down low
weeping and wailing
for Sebinos, the Anaphlystian.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: And Callias they say
The son of Horsescrew
fights naval battles with a lion skin covering his crack.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Could you tell us
Where Pluto lives around here?
We're strangers, just arrived.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: You needn't go far
and don't ask me again,
but know that you've come to the very door.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Pick them up again, my boy.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: This business is nothing
but that old cliché “Zeus' Corinth”—it bugs me!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Onward!
In the sacred round dance of the goddess, in the flower-bearing grove
sporting with all who partake in festival dear to the goddess
I will go with the women and girls
where they dance all night for the goddess, to bring the sacred torch.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Let's march to the flowery meadows,
blooming with roses,
revelling in our fashion
with song and fairest dance
which the blessed
Fates array.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: We alone enjoy the sun
and the light
who have been initiated
and follow the way of piety
towards strangers
and laymen.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, how should I knock on the door now? How?
How do the natives here knock on doors?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Don't waste time, take a bite of the door,
Just like Heracles, since you've got his form and temper.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Hey! porter, porter!

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Who is it?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Heracles the mighty.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: O impious, daring, and most shameless wretch,
O villain, double villain, and arch-villain,
It was you who came before, and stole my dog,
Poor Cerberus! you gagged and seized him,
And then ran off—I was guarding him! but now we've got you,
Thus the black-hearted Stygian rock
and the crag of Acheron dripping with gore
can hold you; and the circling hounds of Cocytus
and Echidna with her hundred heads shall tear
your entrails; your lungs will be attacked by
the Tartesian Eel, your kidneys
bleeding with your very entrails
the Tithrasian Gorgons will rip apart.
To them I will direct my hasty foot.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Hey, what'd you do?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I made a mess. Call the god.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Ridiculous! Quick, get up,
before some stranger sees you!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But I feel faint
Bring me the sponge, and place it near my heart.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Please apply it.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Where? O golden Gods!
Is that where you have your heart?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: It was terrified,
and crept into my bowels down below.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Of Gods and men you surely are the biggest coward.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Who, me?
A coward? how so? Didn't I ask you for the sponge?
Another man would not have acted thus.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What would he do?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: A coward would have lain down flat, and smelt unpleasant—
I stood upright and wiped myself besides.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: A manly act, by Poseidon.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: God, I think so.
But weren't you scared of that rumble of words
and threats?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: God no! I didn't even notice.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well now, since you're so brave and heroic,
you be me, and take my club
and lion skin, if you've got fearless guts.
And I will be the porter in your place.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Give me that stuff quick; I cannot but obey.
Now look upon the Xanthian Heracles,
And see if I will be a coward and lose heart like you.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh no, you'll be a regular whipping-boy of Melite,
Let's go, I'll take up the pack here.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.l: O dearest Heracles, you've returned! Come right in.
When the goddess heard you'd arrived, right off
she had us bake loaves of bread, and boil two or three pots
of ground pea soup; and roast a whole ox;
bake cakes and cookies; do come in.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Fine, I'm much obliged, but...

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.l: By Apollo, I will not
let you go away, since she's also
stewing up some flesh of fowls, and cooked
desserts, and mixed her sweetest wine.
So please come in.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Very nice, but...

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.l: You're kidding.
I won't let go of you. There's also a flute-girl for you
inside, a beauty, and other dancing girls
some two or three.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What'd you say? dancing girls?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Ripe to bursting and freshly plucked.
Come inside, since the cook was just about to take off
the fillets, and the table's coming in.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Go on, and first tell the dancing girls
who are inside that I myself am coming in:
Follow, slave, and bring my baggage.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You, stop! You're not really serious,
since I dressed you up as Heracles for a joke.
Stop fooling around, Xanthias;
Pick the bags back up and bring them along.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What? surely you don't intend to take away from me
what you gave me yourself.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: No maybes, I'm doing it.
Take off the hide.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I'll sue you!
and entrust my case to the gods.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Which gods?
To expect that you—isn't it vain and foolish?
that you, a slave and mortal, could be Alcmena's son?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, never mind, fine; take them, but maybe soon
you'll need me, if god so wills.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: This is the mark of a man
who's got wit and brains and
has sailed around the block a few times:
to roll himself over
to the prospering side
rather than stand like
a graven image, taking a single position.
But to change
for the softer
is the mark of a clever man,
a true Theramenes.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Wouldn't this be a laugh, if
Xanthias, my slave, upturned on
Milesian blankets,
kissing his dancing girl,
asked me for a chamber pot,
and I, looking right at him,
grabbed his cucumber,
and he, being a bully himself,
saw me, and socked me on the jaw
with his fist, knocking out
my front row teeth.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Plathane, Plathane, come here!
Here's the villain that once came to our inn
And ate up sixteen loaves.

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: By Zeus,
That's the very one.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Trouble's here for somebody.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: And twenty boiled beeves, on top of that,
at half a buck apiece.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Some one will catch it now.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Lots of garlic, too.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Surely you jest, good woman;
You don't know what you're saying.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: What! Did you think that,
because you're wearing those booties, I wouldn't recognise you?

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: What else? I've not yet mentioned the pickled fish,
oh no, and the new cheese, the wretch,
that he devoured baskets and all.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Then, when I figured out the price,
He looked straight in my face, and bellowed fierce.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: That's his doing all right, it's his manner everywhere.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Then he drew his sword, and seemed insane.

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: He did! poor woman!

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: We both were terrified,
We ran up to the loft at once;
but he took off—after grabbing our rugs.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: That's his way as well—

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: But we should take some action.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Go on and call my patron Cleon.

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: And if you meet Hyperbolus, summon him for me
so we can rub this guy out.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: Detested throat!
How I'd love to take a rock and smash your molars out,
with which you ate up all my wares.

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: And I could throw you in the deepest pit.

sp.speaker: Pandokeutria
sp.l: And I should like to take a scythe, and slice the throat that swallowed up my tripe.

sp.speaker: Plathane
sp.l: But I'm going after Cleon, who'll deliver a summons
and reel it out of him today.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now may I die, but, Xanthias, I do love you.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I know what you're thinking, I know; but stop, not another word. I won't be Heracles again.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't say that, Xanthias.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: How could I ever be
Alcmene's son, since I'm a slave and mortal too?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I know you're angry, I know, and you've every right to be.
Even if you beat me, I'd never contradict you.
But if I ever take anything from you in time to come,
may I be cut off root and branch! May I myself, my wife, my children perish, and cock-eyed Archedemus, all together!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I accept the oath, and on these terms I'll take them.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Now again it's your job, since
you've taken the robe, which
you had at the start, again
to rejuvenate yourself,
and cast an awful glance,
mindful of the god,
to whom you liken yourself.
But if you're caught babbling
or emit some cowardly sound,
you'll have to pick up
the baggage again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Not bad advice, my friends,
And I just happened to think
this myself.
Since if there's anything good,
he'll try to take this back from me
I know full well.
But nonetheless I'll show
myself manly of heart
and spicy of look.
I think I'll need to, since I hear
just now a knock on the door.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Quick, bind this dogthief,
so he'll pay the penalty. Hurry up!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Trouble's here for somebody.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Go to blazes! Don't come near me!

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Oho, you put up a fight? Ditylas, Skeblias, and Pardocas, come here and fight this guy.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Isn't it awful that this fellow puts up a fight
swiping other people's goods besides?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Just monstrous.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Downright mean and awful.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I swear by God
I'm willing to die, if ever I came here before,
or stole anything of yours that's worth a hair.
And I'll do the noble thing by you.
Here, take this slave of mine, and torture him,
And if you find that I've done wrong, take me out and kill me.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: How may I torture him?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Every way; tie him to a ladder,
hang him, flog him with spikes, flay him,
twist him, pour vinegar up his nose,
pile up loads of bricks, everything else except
Don't beat him with a leek or tender onion.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: A fair offer! And if I should cripple your
boy in the beating, you'll get compensation.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: No, not for me. Just take him away and torture him.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: No, I will do it here; so he'll confess before your eyes
Quick, you, put down your pack, and make sure
you tell no lies.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I forbid anyone
from torturing me, an immortal. Or else
you'll have yourself to blame.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: What'd you say?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I say that I am Dionysus, son of Zeus,
And this man is my slave.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: You hear that?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I do.
So much more reason he should be whipped.
Because, if he is a god, he won't feel it.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, then, since you too claim to be a god:
Why not get hit as many blows as me?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: A fair offer! whichever of us two
You first see cry or noticing at all
being beaten, be sure he's not the God.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: It's for certain you are an honest fellow,
You go for justice. Now strip, you both.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: How will you fairly judge?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Easily;
Blow for blow each one.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Good idea.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: There!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Watch if you see me flinch.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: I already hit you!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: You did not.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: I guess I didn't.
So now I'll go and whack this guy.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, when?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Why, I hit you!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Then why didn't I even sneeze?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: I don't know. I'll try this one again.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Well, hurry up—wahoo!

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: What's this wahoo?
That didn't hurt, did it?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: O no, I just thought
Of the Herculean feast at Diomeia.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: A holy man—and now I've got to go back here.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: O, Whoa!

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: What is it?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I see some horsemen.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: So why are you crying?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Because I smell onions.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Then you don't notice anything?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't mind at all.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Well, in that case, I must go back to this one.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Yow!

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: What is it?

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Pull out this thorn.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: What's going on? Got to go back here.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Apollo, who hast Delos and Pytho...

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: He got hurt; didn't you hear?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Not me, it's just that
I was recalling a verse of Hipponax.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: You're getting nowhere— hit him in the side.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: You're right. Now, stick out that belly!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Poseidon—

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Someone got hurt.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: —who rules the Aegean headlands and in the gray sea's depths—

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: I swear by Demeter that I can't discover
Which of you is the God: but come on in.
My master himself will soon find out,
and Persephone, since they are gods themselves.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now you're making sense. I only wish that you had
done that before I took those whacks.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Muse of the sacred dances, advance and come to enjoy my song,
to see the great throng of people, where wits
sit by the thousand
more honorable than Cleophon, on whose babbling lips
roars terribly
a Thracian swallow
sitting on an alien leaf.
She rumbles her sorrowful nightingale's song, since he will perish
even in case of a tie.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: It is right and just for our sacred chorus to advise and teach what's good for the city. So first it seems best to us
to equalize the citizens and take away their fears.
And if anyone went astray, tripped by the wrestling moves of Phrynichus,
I say it should be possible for those who slipped up then
to plead their cause and erase their previous mistakes.
Because it's disgraceful that those who fought just once at sea
should suddenly be Plataeans and masters instead of slaves.
No, even this I couldn't say wasn't well and good,
in fact, I praise it. It's the only sensible thing you did.
But it's also fair, for people who've fought so much at sea
with you, as did their fathers, people who are related to your race
that you let pass their one misfortune, as they request.
But letting up on your anger, you who are wisest in nature,
let's gladly make everyone our kinsman
and full-fledged citizens too, who's ever fought for us at sea.
But if we swell up with pride at this, and give the city airs,
especially since we're in the grasp of the waves,
in time to come again we'll get a reputation for stupidity.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: If I'm a fair judge of the life and habits of a man who will yet come to grief,
not long will this annoying ape
Cleigenes the tiny,
the nastiest bathman of all who rule the ash-mixed
polluted soda lye
and the Cimolian earth,
not long will he be around. But knowing this
he's no pacifist, lest he ever be stripped while
wandering drunk without his staff.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Many times it seems to us the city has done
the same thing with the best and the brightest of its citizens
as with the old coinage and the new gold currency.
For these, not counterfeit at all,
but the finest it seems of all coins,
and the only ones of the proper stamp, of resounding metal
amongst Greeks and foreigners everywhere,
we never use, but the inferior bronze ones instead,
minted just yesterday or the day before with the basest stamp.
So too the citizens whom we know to be noble and virtuous,
and righteous and true men of quality
and trained in the palaestra and dancing and music,
these we despise, but the brazen foreigners and redheads
worthless sons of worthless fathers, these we use for everything,
these latest parvenus, whom the city before this
wouldn't have lightly used even for random scapegoats.
But now, you dimwits, change your ways,
and employ the good ones again. And if you succeed,
it's praiseworthy. But if you stumble, at least you'll hang from a respectable tree—
So wise men will think, if anything happens to you.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: By Zeus our Saviour, a real gentleman
is your master.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Of course he's a real gentleman,
he only knows how to drink and screw.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: But not to beat you then and there when it was proved
that you're the slave but claimed to be the master!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: He'd sure regret it.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: That's a right slavish thing
you did just now, the kind of thing I like to do myself.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Beg pardon, you like that?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Even more, I'm practically in ecstasy
When I curse my master behind his back.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What about your grumbling, when after getting
a good beating you run outside?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: I love that too.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And what of meddling?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: It's like nothing else I know, by God.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Zeus of Family Ties! And eavesdropping on the masters
when they gossip?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: It drives me even crazier.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What about blabbing it all to outsiders?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Who, me?
God, when I do that, I stain my pants.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Phoebus Apollo! Put your right hand there,
Let me kiss you—you kiss me too, and tell me
By Zeus, who is our fellow whipping boy,
What's all this noise inside and shouting
and abuse?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: That's Euripides and Aeschylus.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Huh?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Big, big trouble's stirring
among the dead, and nasty civil war.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: There is a custom established here,
in all the great and noble arts
that the best man in his own field of talent
gets his meals in the Town Hall,
and the seat next to Pluto...

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I get it.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Until someone wiser in the art arrives
Than he, and then must he give way.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: So why has this disturbed Aeschylus?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: He held the chair of tragedy,
As the mightiest in that art.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And who does now?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Why, when Euripides came down, he started showing off
to the muggers and the pickpockets,
parricides, and burglars,
and that's the majority in Hades—and listening to
his speeches pro and con, and twists and turns,
they went crazy and hailed him the wisest.
Then he, all excited, claimed the throne
where Aeschylus was sitting.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And wasn't he bombarded?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Lord no, the plebs cried out to have a trial,
to see which was the better dramatist.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: The crowd of rascals?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Oh yes, as high as heaven.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Didn't Aeschylus have others to take his side?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: The best's a small group, just like here.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And what is Pluto planning to do?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: To hold the contest right away, and a trial
and test of their skill.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And how is it then
that Sophocles didn't claim the throne as well?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Not him, by Zeus, but he kissed Aeschylus
When he arrived, and shook his hand,
And yielded the chair to him.
Now he intends, so says Cleidemides,
to sit out in reserve. And if Aeschylus wins,
he'll stay put; if not, he said he'd fight
against Euripides for the sake of his art.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: So this thing will really happen?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Yes, just a little later,
and here there'll be an awful commotion.
For poetry will be measured out on scales!

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: What? They're going to weigh tragedy by the ounce?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: And they'll bring out rulers and verbal yardsticks,
and flexible frames,

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Then they'll be making bricks?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: And bevels and wedges. Because Euripides
says he'll test the plays word by word.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: I guess Aeschylus is taking it pretty hard.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: Well, he lowered his head and cast a bullish glance.

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: And who's to be the judge?

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: That was difficult.
You'll find a shortage of sophisticated men.
Aeschylus didn't get along with the Athenians—

sp.speaker: Xanthias
sp.l: Maybe he thought most of them were crooks.

sp.speaker: Aeacus
sp.l: And he considered the rest trash for judging
the essence of poets: so to your master
they turned, since he has experience in the art.
But let's go in; for when masters
are in a hurry, it means trouble for us.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Surely the dreadful thunderer will feel wrath within him
as he looks at the rival whetting his babbling tusk.
Then his eyes will spin with awful madness.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: There will be the helmet-blazing strife of horse-crested phrases;
Axle-splinterings as the chisel-working fellow defends himself
against the horse-galloping utterances of the mind-building man.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Bristling the shaggy-necked mane of his natural-hair crest,
Knitting his terrible brow, bellowing, he will launch
bolt-fastened utterances, ripping them apart board by board
with gigantic blast of breath.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Then the mouth-worker, tester of phrases, smooth
tongue, unfurling, stirring the reins of envy,
dissecting the utterances, will quibble away
the great labor of his lungs.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: I will never yield the chair, no more advice;
For I claim to be this man's superior in the art.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Why are you silent, Aeschylus? You hear what he says.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: First he'll put on solemn airs, just as so often
he used to pull those hoaxes in his tragedies.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: My good sir, don't talk so high and mighty.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: I know him well, and have long examined him,
creator of crude characters, stubborn-mouthed,
he's got an unbridled, uncontrolled, ungated mouth
uncircumlocuitous, brag-bundle-voiced.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Is that right, you child of the garden goddess?
You call me that, you gossip-gathering
beggar-making son of a rag-stitcher?
You'll be sorry for saying that.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Cease, Aeschylus,
Don't heat up your innards with wrath so angrily.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Oh no, not before I thoroughly expose this
cripple-creator for the braggart that he is.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: A sheep, a black sheep, boys, bring one out,
for a typhoon is fixing to let loose!

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You collector of Cretan arias
bringing unholy wedlocks to our art—

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Hold on there, much-distinguished Aeschylus:
And you, you rogue Euripides, get out of the way
of this hailstorm, if you are wise,
lest with some heady phrase he crack your skull
in anger and spill out your Telephus.
And you, don't get angry, Aeschylus, but gently
test and be tested; it's just not proper
for poets to abuse each other like fishwives.
But you roar like an oak on fire.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: I am prepared, and do not delay,
to bite, be bitten first, if that's his preference,
as to the lines and lyrics, the sinews of a tragedy,
I swear by Zeus, by Peleus, and by Aeolus,
by MeIeager too, and even more, by Telephus.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And what do you plan to do? Speak, Aeschylus.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I didn't want to join in battle here;
Our combat will not be on equal terms.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How so?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: My Poetry did not die with me,
as his has died with him, so he'll have it to recite.
But nonetheless since you prefer, it must be done.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Come now, someone bring incense and fire,
So I can pray before the show of wits
to judge this contest most aesthetically.
And you, sing a song to the Muses.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Ye Nine virgin daughters of Zeus, blessed
Muses, who look down upon the subtle-speaking clever wits
of phrase-forging men, when to strife
they come, debating with fiercely studied, crooked wrestling holds,
come to observe the power
of most awesome mouths to provide
sayings and sawdust of words.
For now the great contest of skill is getting down to business.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now, both say a prayer before speaking your verses.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Demeter, nourisher of my mind,
grant that I be worthy of thy mysteries!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now you too take and offer incense.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Fine,
but I have other gods I pray to.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Your own private ones, newly minted?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Yes, indeed.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, pray away to these private Gods.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: O air, my sustenance, and pivot of my tongue,
and intelligence, and olfactory nostrils,
may I stoutly refute whatever words I seize!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Truly do we desire
to hear from these clever men, what
warpath of words you walk on.
For their tongue is savage
and the temper of both is not without boldness
nor their wits lethargic.
It seems likely to expect
that the one will utter something urbane
and finely honed,
while the other, pulling up by the root
his arguments to attack with,
will scatter the many wallows of words.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now you must talk as fast as you can, and see that you both speak
elegantly, and no similes or the things someone else might say.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Well, of myself and what sort of poet I am,
I will tell at the end: but first I'll prove that this man
was an impostor and a cheat, and how he took the spectators and used to fool the dupes reared with Phrynichos.
First, he'd wrap up and sit down someone or other,
An Achilles, or Niobe, not showing the face,
a facade of tragedy, not mumbling so much as this.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's right, they didn't.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And then the chorus boomed
four strings of lyric in a row nonstop: but they kept quiet.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: And l enjoyed their silence; that pleased me
no less than the babblers now.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Because you were stupid,
no doubt about it.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I think so too. Why did the so-and-so do this?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: From fraudulence, so the spectator would sit there waiting
for when Niobe would say something. And the play would go on.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh what a villain! How I was fooled by him!
Why do you stretch and act uncomfortable?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Because I'm convicting him.
And then after he pulled this cheap trick, and the play
was already half over, he'd speak a dozen bullish words
With eyebrows, crests, some awful witch-faced things,
Unknown to the audience.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Woe is me, alas.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Quiet.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Yet not a thing he said was clear—

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Don't saw your teeth.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: But Scamanders, or trenches, or shield-adorning
bronze-beaten griffon-eagles and horse-cliffed phrases,
which it was not easy to construe.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Ye gods! As for me,
“one night did I pass sleepless all the while,”
wondering what sort of bird the yellow hipporooster was.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You blockhead, it's a symbol engraved on ships.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I thought it was Eryxis, Philoxenus' son.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Then, did you have to create a rooster in tragedy?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You god-detested wretch! What sort of things did
you used to compose?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Not hipporoosters, by God, nor goat-stags, like you,
which they depict on Persian tapestries.
But when I first received the art from you,
she was swollen from bombast and ponderous diction,
at once I slimmed her down and took off weight
with versicles and strolls and laxative roots,
giving a dose of drivel strained from books.
Then I nursed it back with monodies—

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: —mixing in Cephisophon.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Then I didn't say whatever nonsense occurred to me, nor knead in what I fell upon,
But the character who came out first would straightway
tell the background of the play.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Better than your own, by Zeus.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Then from the opening words I permitted nothing idle; my woman spoke, as did the slave as well,
Or master, maiden, or old woman.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Then really
shouldn't you be put to death for daring this?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: No, by Apollo,
For this was a democratic thing I did.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Let it go, sir,
It's not best for you to digress on that point.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Then, I taught these folks to speak up...

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I'll say,
I wish before that lesson you had split down the middle.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: ...And the introduction of subtle rules and squared-off words,
to think, to see, to understand, to love to twist, to connive,
to suspect the worst, to overthink all things...

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I'll say.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: ...Introducing domestic matters which we're used to and understand,
on which I could be tested. For these folks are knowledgeable,
and could have criticized my art. But I didn't toss off boasts,
drawing them away from common sense, and I didn't scare them,
creating Cycnuses and Memnons of the bell-cheeked steeds.
You'll recognize the disciples of both this fellow and myself:
His are Phormisios and manic Meganeitos
Sons of long-beard lancers, pine-tree flesh rippers,
but mine are Cleitophon and Theramenes the dandy.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Theramenes? A clever fellow, an all-round wonder;
If he runs into trouble and happens to be close by
He's thrown clear of the trouble, no Chian but a Kian.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Well, to ponder such things, I
instructed these folks here,
putting logic in my art
and scrutiny, so now they notice
everything and know through and through
most especially how to run
the household better than before,
and they inquire, “How's this doing?
Where's this? Who took that?”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Yes, by gods! In fact, now
every single Athenian goes inside
and yells to his servants
and asks, “Where's my pot?
Who's eaten off the head
of my sardine; My bowl
of yesteryear—has it perished?
Where is yesterday's garlic?
Who nibbled at the olive?”
Before now the biggest dummies
gaping mamma's boys
would just sit like blockheads.

sp.speaker: Chorus.
sp.l: See'st thou this, shining Achilles?
Come now, what will you say to that? Just be sure
that your temper doesn't get hold of you
and carry you out of bounds.
For he has made terrible accusations.
But come, O noble one,
Do not contradict him in anger,
but reef in your sails,
use only the tips,
then little by little you'll bring her to
and watch out for when
you may catch a calmed and gentle breeze.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Oh, you who first of the Greeks built solemn phrases
and decorated tragic nonsense, take heart and let loose your spout.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I am indignant at this encounter, and it gripes my guts,
if I have to argue against this fellow—but so that he can't say I was helpless,—
Answer me, why should one admire a poet?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: For cleverness, and giving good advice, since we improve
the people in the cities.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: So if you haven't done this,
but turned them from fine and decent types into villains,
what will you say you deserve to suffer?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Death: don't ask him.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Consider now what kind of men he first received from me
if they were generous and six feet tall, no runaway citizens,
no loafers, rascals, like now, nor miscreants,
but men who breathed spears and lances, white-crested helmets,
and headgear, and greaves and sevenfold oxhide tempers.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: This is really getting bad: he'll crush me with his helmet-making.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And what did you do to teach men to be so noble?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Speak, Aeschylus; don't be a stubborn highfalutin' sorehead.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I composed a drama filled with Mars.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Which one?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: The Seven against Thebes.
Everyone who saw it fell in love with being fierce.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That was a bad thing you did, since you made the Thebans
more courageous in war. For that at least get whacked.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You could have trained for this as well, but you weren't so inclined.
Then, producing The Persians after that, I taught them to yearn
to beat the enemy; this finest feat did I honor.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, I rejoiced when you lamented for the death of Darius,
and the chorus straightway clapped their hands like this and said, “Ee-ow!”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: This is the stuff poets should work on. Just look right from the start
how useful the noble race of poets has been.
For Orpheus taught us rites and to refrain from killing,
And Musaeus taught the cures of illness and oracles, and Hesiod
the working of the land, harvest seasons, plowing. Divine Homer,
Where did he get honor and glory if not from teaching useful things,
battle lines, courageous deeds, men's armory?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But I bet he didn't
teach Pantacles, that clumsy oaf. The other day, when he was parading,
He fastened his helmet on first and then was going to tie on the crest!

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: And many other brave men too, of which the hero Lamachos was one;
from Homer, my brain composed many great feats of valor,
of Patrocluses, lion-hearted Teucrians, so I could rouse the citizenry
to strive to equal them, when it hears the call to arms.
But by God, I never created whores like Phaedra and Sthenoboea
No one's ever known me to write about any woman in love.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: No sir, you've got nothing to do with Aphrodite.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: And may she stay away!
But she settled down on you and yours in force,
and destroyed your very self.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: By God, that she did.
What you used to do to other mens's wives, you got hit with yourself.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And how have my Stheneboeas harmed the state, you wretch?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Since you persuaded noble ladies, wives of noble men
to drink hemlock out of shame because of people like that Bellerophon of yours.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: So did I make up some non-existent story about Phaedra?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: No, it existed. But a poet should conceal wickedness, not bring it forward and teach it. For little boys
have a teacher who advises them, and grown-ups have poets.
We have a serious obligation to speak of honorable things.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: So, if you speak to us of Lycabettuses
and the heights of Parnassuses, this is “teaching honorable things”,
when a poet ought to speak in human terms?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You fiend! It is the compelling power
of great thoughts and ideas to engender phrases of equal size.
And anyway it is proper that demigods speak in grander terms.
For they also wear much finer clothes.
What I so nobly exhibited you defiled.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: What did I do?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: First you dressed the kingly types in rags, so
they'd look pitiful to the audience.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And what harm did I do by that?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Because of that, no wealthy man was willing to fund the navy,
but wrapped in rags he weeps and claims he's poor.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: By Demeter, yes, but wearing a tunic of pure wool underneath!
And if he fooled 'em with that story, he'd pop up in the fish market.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Then again, you taught them to practice drivel and gossip,
which emptied the gymnasia and ruined the butts
of our prattling youths, and persuaded the Paralian crews
to argue with their officers. But when I was alive,
they knew nothing but to call for grits and sing Yo-ho!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Yessir, and fart in the face of their rowing mate,
dump on their mess partner, go ashore and rob someone.
But now he argues and doesn't row, and sails to and fro.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Of what crimes is he not guilty?
Didn't he show pimps,
women giving birth in temples,
sleeping with their brothers,
claiming that life is not life?
And then our state
is filled with these bureaucrats
and oafish democratic apes
always cheating the people,
and there's no one able to carry the torch
any more because of lack of training.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: No sir, not any more! So that I laughed
myself dry at the Panathenaic games, when
some slow guy ran, hunched over,
pale, drunk, left behind
and doing miserably. And then the folks of the Ceramicus
at the gates hit his
stomach, ribs, sides, butt,
and he, getting whacked with their hands,
broke wind,
blew out the torch and ran away.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Great the event, abundant the strife, grand the war that advances.
So it's hard work to choose
when one strains violently,
while the other can twist around and bear down sharply.
But don't just sit where you are.
For the attacks of wit are many and varied.
So for what you have to quarrel over,
speak out, lay on, beat up,
the old stuff and the new,
and dare to say something subtle and smart.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: But if you're both afraid that our spectators lack a certain amount of knowledge, so as
not to appreciate the fine points of what you say,
don't worry about that, since that is no longer the case.
For they are seasoned veterans
and each one has a book and understands the clever stuff.
Their minds are superior anyway,
but now they're really sharpened.
So fear not, but
scrutinize every topic, for the audience's sake at least, since they're so sophisticated.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: All right then, I'll turn to your prologues themselves,
so that first of all I can test the first section
of this clever poet's tragedy.
For he was unclear in the explanation of events.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Which one of his will you test?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Quite a lot.
First, recite to me the start of the Oresteia.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now silence, every one! Speak, Aeschylus.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Subterranean Hermes, guardian of my father's realms,
Become my savior and my ally, in answer to my prayer.
For I am come and do return to this my land.”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Do you have something to criticize in this?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: More than a dozen.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: But the whole thing wasn't more than three lines.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And each one has twenty mistakes.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I warn you to keep quiet, Aeschylus—if not,
on top of these three verses you'll wind up owing more.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: ME be quiet for HIM?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: If you take my advice.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Right off he made mistakes as high as heaven.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: You see that you're ranting!

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Doesn't bother me in the least.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: What mistakes do you claim I make?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Repeat it from the start one more time.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Subterranean Hermes, guardian of my father's realms,”—

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Doesn't Orestes say this at the grave
Of his dead father?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I grant that much.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Well, seeing that his father died a death
of violence, slain by a woman's hand,
in a secret plot, how can he say that Hermes guarded anything?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Not that one, but the Luck-Bringer
Hermes he called “Subterranean”, and he made it clear by saying
that he has this function from his father.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: You made an even bigger mistake than I imagined.
For if he has this underground junction from his father—

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Then he'd be a grave robber on his father's side.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Dionysus, the wine you drink doesn't smell too good.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Recite another for him. And you watch out for damage.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Become my savior and my ally, in answer to my prayer.
For I am come and do return to this my land.”

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Sage Aeschylus has said the same thing twice.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: How twice?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Look at his words and I'll tell you.
“I am come to this my land”, he says, “and do return.”
To come is the same thing as to return.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Right! just as if a man said to his neighbour,
Lend me a dish, and, if you please, a saucer.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: That's not so at all, you blabbermouth,
It's not the same, but uses the best choice of words.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: How so? Show me what you're talking about.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: To come to a land is for someone who owns a fatherland.
An exile both arrives and does return.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well done, by Apollo ! What do you say, Euripides?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: I deny Orestes returned home ,
For he came secretly, without permission of the authorities.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well done, by Hermes! But I don't know what you mean.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Continue now with another.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Yes, do go on,
Aeschylus, hurry up. And you look out for something bad.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “At this tomb-mound do I my sire entreat
To hear and listen.”

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: This is another thing he repeats.
“To hear and listen” are clearly the same thing.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Because he was speaking to the dead, you idiot,
whom we don't even reach with the triple lament.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Well, how did you make prologues?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: I'll tell you.
And if I ever I say the same word twice, or if you see padding
in there irrelevant to the plot, spit on me.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Speak, come on. For I cannot but hear
the correctness of your prologue's diction.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “At first was Oedipus a prosperous man.”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Good Lord, not at all; he was ill-starred by nature.
Before his birth Apollo said that he
would kill his father, even before he was begotten!
How could he at first have been a lucky man?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Then he became in turn the wretchedest of mortals.”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: No, not at all; he never ceased to be.
How's that? Since as soon as he was born,
they exposed him in a broken pot at wintertime,
so he wouldn't grow up to be his father's murderer.
Then he dragged himself to Polybus on swollen feet,
after that he married an old woman, though young himself,
and on top of that she was his own mother.
Then he blinded himself.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: So he was happy then,
at least if he had campaigned with Erasinides.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: You're fooling; I craft my prologues beautifully.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Oh really? Well, by Zeus, not word by word will I grate
each phrase of yours, but with the Gods' help,
I'll demolish your prologues with a little oil flask.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: My prologues with an oil flask?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: A single one.
For you compose in such a way that everything fits in,
a little fleece, a little oil flask and little bag,
in your iambics. I'll prove it here and now.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Look here! You'll prove it?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I say so.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well, then, you've got to speak.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Aegyptus, so the widespread rumor runs,
With fifty children in a long-oared boat,
Landing near Argos”—

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What was this “oil flask”? You'll be sorry!
Recite for him another prologue, so I can see once more.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Dionysus, who with thyrsus wands and fawnskins
bedecked amidst the pines on Mt. Parnassus
bounds dancing...”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Alas, again we have been stricken by that flask.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: It won't be a problem. For to this
prologue he won't be able to attach that flask.
“No man exists, who's altogether blest,
Either nobly sired he has no livelihood
Or else base-born he ...”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Euripides!

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: What is it?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I think you should pull in your sails;
that oil flask is going to blow up quite a storm.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: By Demeter, I wouldn't think of it.
For this one here will knock it away from him.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Go on and recite another then, but keep away from the flask!

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Abandoning the town of Sidon, Cadmus,
Agenor's son,...”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: My fine fellow, buy the flask;
so he can't smash our prologues.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: What!
I should buy it from him?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: If you take my advice.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Oh no; for I have many prologues to recite,
Where he can't tack on a flask.
“To Pisa Pelops, son of Tantalus,
Borne on swift coursers”—

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You see, he stuck on the flask again.
But, dear sir, pay him now by all means.
You'll get it for an obol, nice and neat.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Not yet, by Zeus; I still have plenty left.
“From the land once Oeneus”—

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Let me say the whole line first!
“From the land once Oeneus reaped a plenteous crop,
The first fruits offering”—

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Lost his little oil flask!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: In the midst of sacrificing? Who swiped it?

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Leave it be, sir, just let him speak to this—
“Zeus, as once was spoke in very truth”—

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: You'll get killed, for he'll say “Lost his little oil flask!” This oil flask, it grows on your prologues
like warts on the eyes.
For God's sake turn to his lyrics.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: All right; I have ways to show how bad
a songwriter he is and always makes them just the same.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Whatever will happen now?
I can only imagine
what complaints he will make
against the man who wrote by far the most
and finest songs up to now.
(I wonder how
he'll criticize this man
the Dionysiac lord
And I fear for him.)

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Quite marvelous songs, as this will soon make clear.
For I'll condense all his songs into one point.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Well then, I'll grab some pebbles and keep score.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “O Phthian Achilles, if you hear the manslaughtering
crash, ah, why do you not come to our aid?
To Hermes we, the ancestral race, pay homage by the lake,
crash, ah, why do you not come to our aid?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: That's two crashes for you, Aeschylus.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Most glorious of the Achaeans, far-ruling son of Atreus, learn of me,
crash, ah, why do you not come to our aid?”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: This is your third crash, Aeschylus.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Be still. The Bee-nuns draw near to open the temple of Artemis.
Crash, ah, why do you not come to our aid?
I am charged with uttering the heroes' fateful command of the journey,
crash, ah, why do you not come to our aid?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: King Zeus, what a load of crashes!
I for one want to go to the bathhouse,
For my kidneys are swollen with all this crashing.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Don't, before you hear another set of odes
assembled from his melodies for the lyre.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Go on, continue, but leave out the crash.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “How the twin-throned power of the Achaeans, of Grecian youth,
Tophlattothrattoplilattothrat,
sends the sphinx, unlucky presiding dog,
Tophlattothrattophlattothrat,
The swooping bird with spear and avenging hand
Tophlattothrattophlattothrat,
Granting to the headlong sky-flying dogs to meet
Tophlattothrattophlattothrat,
The united force against Ajax
Tophlattothrattophlattothrat,

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: What is this phlattothrat? Is it from Marathon, or
where did you assemble these songs of a rope-twister?

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Well, to a fine place from a fine place did I
bring them, lest I be seen garnering from the same meadow as Phrynichos.
But this guy gets them from everywhere, from little whores,
Meletus' drinking songs, Carian flute solos,
Dirges, dances. This will all be made clear immediately.
Someone bring in a lyre. And yet, what need
of a lyre for this guy? Where's the girl who clacks the castanets? Hither, Muse of Euripides,
for whom these songs are appropriate to sing.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: This Muse never did the Lesbian thing, oh no..

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Halcyon kingfishers, who by the sea's everflowing
waves do chatter,
moistening the surface of your wings with damp
drops bedewing,
and ye spiders who in the corners under the roof
wi-yi-yi-yi-yi-yind with your fingers
loom-stretched threads
the cares of the shuttle bard,
where the flute-loving dolphin was leaping
by the blue-peaked prows
oracles and stades.
Wine-blooming joy of the vine
painkilling spiral of grapes,
cast your arms about me, child.
....You see this foot?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I see it.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Well, do you see this one?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I see it.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: Well, you write this sort of thing
and dare to criticize my lyrics,
you composer in the twelve tone style of Cyrene?
So much for his songs. I still want
to scrutinize the manner of his melodies.
Oh dark-shining night's
gloom, what woeful dream
do you send to me, from unseen Hades'
vestibules, possessing a soulless
soul, child
of black night, hair-raising horrible
sight, black-corpse-shrouded, murder, murder
envisioning, with long fingernails?
Now servants, light my lamp
Draw moisture in pitchers from the rivers, and heat water,
that I might wash away the divine dream.
O Marine Spirit,
So that's it. O Housemates,
Behold these portents!
Snatching my rooster
Glyce has fled.
Mountain-born Nymphs,
O Mania, help!
But I, the wretched one
happened to be performing my
tasks, the spindle full of thread
wi-yi-yinding in my hands
making a skein, so that
at dawn to the market
I could bring it to sell.
But it has flown away, flown away into the air
on the nimblest tips of its wings
but to me it left woes, woes,
and tears, tears from my eyes
I shed, shed, oh wretched me!
Now O Cretans, sons of Ida,
take your bows and come to the rescue
bestir your limbs and circle the house.
And also may Child Dictynna, Artemis the fair,
bring her doggies and come to my house by all means.
And you, daughter of Zeus, upholding twin
torches most piercing in your hands,
Hecate, shine me towards Glyce's
so I can go in and catch her in the act.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Stop with the songs already.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: I've had enough, too.
For now I want to bring him to the scale
which alone will put our poetry to the test.
For it will prove the weight of our phrases.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Then come here, if I really have to do this,
to deal with poets just like selling cheese.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.l: Painstaking are the men of wit,
For once again here's another marvel,
brand new, full of the unusual,
who else could have thought it up?
Oh my, I'd never, not if anybody
I ran into told me,
have believed it, but I would have thought
he was talking nonsense.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Come on and stand beside the balance pans.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus and Euripides
sp.l: Here we are!

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now, each of you grab hold and speak a verse,
and don't let go till I yell “Cuckoo!”

sp.speaker: Euripides and Aeschylus
sp.l: We holding on.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Now recite the line into the scales.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Would that the Argive bark had never winged...”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Stream of Spercheius, haunts of grazing kine...”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Cuckoo! It's released. And much further down
goes this man's side.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Whatever is the reason?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Because he introduced a stream; like fabric salesmen
he made his verse wet just like the wool.
But you put in a winged word.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Well, let him say something else and match me.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Grab hold again.

sp.speaker: Aeschylus and Euripides
sp.l: All set.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Speak!

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Persuasion has no other shrine save speech.”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Death is the only God that loves not bribes...”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Let go, let go! This one's is tilting once again.
For he inserted Death, weightiest of ills.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: And I Persuasion, a saying beautifully expressed.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Persuasion is but light, and makes no sense.
But this time find some other ponderous line
that will pull down on your side, something high and mighty.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: Tell me, where oh where do I have something like that?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: “Achilles threw snake eyes and a four”—
Please speak, since this is your last weigh-in.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: “Heavy with iron was the club his right hand seized.”

sp.speaker: Aeschylus
sp.l: “Chariot on chariot, corpse on corpse.”

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: He fooled you again this time.

sp.speaker: Euripides
sp.l: In what way?

sp.speaker: Dionysus
sp.l: Two chariots and two corpses he put in,
